This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 29-2012.01, Histology Technicians: preparing histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists; workers may assist with research studies. Official scope: Prepare histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. May assist with research studies. O*NET lists the following core tasks (9 tasks are listed, with the first 5 displayed by default): cutting body-tissue sections with microtomes for microscopic examination; embedding tissue specimens in paraffin blocks or impregnating them with wax; mounting tissue specimens on glass slides; staining tissue specimens with dyes or other chemicals to make cellular details visible under a microscope; and freezing tissue specimens. Common titles include Histology Technician, Histologic Technician, Histologist, Clinical Histology Technician, and Histology Coordinator. Coverage note: O*NET explicitly labels the U.S. wage and employment data on its 29-2012.01 page as covering the broader parent occupation, Clinical Laboratory Technologists and Technicians, not this exact occupation. This page accurately labels parent-occupation coverage and does not extrapolate it as this occupation's starting pay. In the U.S., the occupation is in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed), 6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0). This page does not extrapolate U.S. coverage to job titles, qualifications, or wages in mainland China.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional histological-specimen processing task package, solely for practicing the process and representing no real institution, specimen, or data. Draft a plan covering: (1) how to use a fictional specimen-processing work order and process instructions to structure assistance with tissue-specimen processing: specimen and case identifiers; fixation, dehydration, clearing and wax infiltration; embedding, sectioning and mounting; staining and coverslipping; reagents and consumables; biosafety and chemical protection; equipment, temperature control and deadlines; and exceptions, rework and specimen traceability. Specify missing information to obtain: specimen condition and clinical requirements, process and reagent versions, safety, biosafety and chemical requirements, equipment condition, and testing deadlines. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional specimen and process record: fields and definitions, specimen and case identifiers, reagents and batches, processing, sectioning and staining parameters, quality, exceptions and rework, and original records and revision trails. (3) How to write a handover-ready shift and specimen-processing summary: specimen and case—processing, sectioning and staining—quality and exceptions—outstanding items and recommendations. (4) How to record and retain specimen and testing data, distinguishing public information from protected case information and controlled process materials. (5) How to pause, reassess, isolate, and report upon discovering specimen mismatches, biosafety, chemical, equipment or quality risks, matters beyond job authority, or a need to stop. Use public materials and simulated data, never real institutional or case data.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 29-2012.01 has interest code RIC (Realistic–Investigative–Conventional): Realistic means hands-on instrument and equipment operation; Investigative means analyzing problems through evidence and technology; Conventional means organizing information and data and maintaining order under procedures and rules. Core activities include making decisions and solving problems (76), documenting and recording information (73), communicating with supervisors, peers or subordinates (72), inspecting equipment, structures or materials (72), and monitoring processes, materials or surroundings (72). Work context shows extremely high accuracy demands (92% extremely important), extremely serious consequences of error (60% extremely serious, 20% very serious), common contaminant exposure (80% daily), common hazardous-equipment exposure (64% daily), collaboration with laboratory colleagues (36% constant contact with others, 32% most of the time), and substantial time pressure (71% daily). If you are willing to work hands-on with specimens, instruments, and reagents, thoroughly manage processes, parameters, quality, and records, and take responsibility for specimen integrity, reliable results, and operational safety, the occupation's daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports the following for 29-2012.01, based on work context and tasks: extremely high accuracy demands (92% extremely important); extremely serious consequences of error (60% extremely serious, 20% very serious); common contaminant exposure (80% daily); common hazardous-equipment exposure (64% daily); common exposure to disease or infection (44% daily); and substantial time pressure (71% daily). This occupation works with tissue specimens, reagents, sections, staining, and instruments. A specimen mismatch or mislabeling, improper biosafety or chemical handling, loss of instrument or process control, or sectioning or staining quality deviation can cause incorrect results, affect diagnosis, expose personnel, and create quality and compliance risks. O*NET places it in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed), 6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0). Its education section reports 48% requiring an associate's or other two-year degree, 16% a postsecondary certificate, and 12% a high school diploma or equivalent (the page lists these three items). Growth is Slower than average (parent-occupation coverage), with no Bright Outlook label. If high precision and low error tolerance are difficult for you, you struggle to work amid biosafety and chemical exposure and testing deadlines, or you are unwilling to take responsibility for specimen integrity, reliable results, and operational safety, treat these as practical costs.

Responsibility check | Actual fit depends on accomplishing three things within the same specimen-processing task: doing the technical work properly—following processes and work orders for fixation, dehydration, wax infiltration, embedding, sectioning, mounting, staining, and coverslipping to produce usable sections and specimen and process records; controlling safety, compliance, and boundaries—working and keeping records under biosafety, chemical, personal-protection, equipment, temperature-control, and deadline requirements, distinguishing public information from protected case information and controlled process materials and handling them under policy, and never reporting results or acting beyond authority without authorization; and accepting defined job responsibilities—being accountable for your own specimen processing, sectioning, staining, and records, while referring matters beyond job authority or involving diagnosis, reporting, or major safety issues to the appropriate role or institution under policy. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as preparing a specimen-processing plan and process and quality records for a fictional work order, or reviewing a response to a specimen mismatch or equipment or quality abnormality, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | Histology Technicians on this page is the exact O*NET occupation 29-2012.01, Histology Technicians. Work falls into several categories: (i) Specimens and preparation—freezing tissue specimens, embedding them in paraffin blocks or impregnating them with wax, and operating computerized laboratory equipment to dehydrate, decalcify, or microincinerate tissue samples. (ii) Sectioning and mounting—cutting body-tissue sections with microtomes for microscopic examination and mounting tissue specimens on glass slides. (iii) Staining and coverslipping—staining tissue specimens with dyes or other chemicals to make cellular details visible under a microscope and loading slides into staining equipment. (iv) Equipment and archiving—maintaining laboratory equipment such as microscopes, microtomes, immunostainers, tissue processors, embedding centers and water baths, and archiving diagnostic materials such as histological slides and paraffin blocks. (v) Quality and records—recording processing, sectioning and staining parameters under processes and quality standards, identifying abnormalities, and reporting them.

Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves three types of requirements. First, technology and quality: processing, sectioning, staining, and archiving must follow processes and current standards, with specimen, process, and quality records. Second, safety and occupational health: biosafety, infectious substances, chemicals, personal protection, waste, equipment, and temperature control must meet biosafety and occupational-health requirements. Third, information and compliance: collection, use, and retention of case information and process materials must meet personal-information protection, medical-quality, and traceability requirements. All are subject to currently effective versions and competent-authority and institutional requirements.

Records and collaboration | Under laboratory quality, biosafety, and information-management policies, record work orders, specimen and case identifiers, reagents and batches, processing, sectioning and staining parameters, quality, exceptions, rework, specimen traceability, original records, and revision trails. Verify specimens and results with colleagues, pathologists, clinical staff, and quality and safety personnel; promptly isolate and report abnormalities.

Workers use specimen-processing and instrument-operation skills and quality awareness within job authority, taking responsibility for specimen integrity, sectioning and staining quality, and operational safety, but not pathology diagnosis. Workers must not issue conclusions in their own name on matters beyond their qualifications, such as pathology diagnoses, medical-quality determinations, or classification of biosafety incidents.

entries.answer: Histology Technicians on this page is the exact O*NET occupation 29-2012.01, Histology Technicians: preparing histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists; workers may assist with research studies. The page lists 9 tasks. The most important include cutting body-tissue sections with microtomes for microscopic examination, embedding tissue specimens in paraffin blocks or impregnating them with wax, mounting tissue specimens on glass slides, staining tissue specimens with dyes or other chemicals to make cellular details visible under a microscope, and freezing tissue specimens. Common titles include Histology Technician, Histologic Technician, Histologist, and Clinical Histology Technician.

subject.name: Histology Technicians
subject.summary: Histology Technicians corresponds to the exact O*NET/SOC occupation 29-2012.01, Histology Technicians: preparing histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists; workers may assist with research studies. Core tasks include cutting body-tissue sections with microtomes for microscopic examination, embedding tissue specimens in paraffin blocks or impregnating them with wax, mounting tissue specimens on glass slides, staining tissue specimens with dyes or other chemicals to make cellular details visible under a microscope, and freezing tissue specimens. Common job titles include Histology Technician, Histologic Technician, Histologist, and Clinical Histology Technician. Official scope: Prepare histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. May assist with research studies. Coverage note: O*NET explicitly labels the wage and employment data presented on its 29-2012.01 page as covering the broader parent occupation, Clinical Laboratory Technologists and Technicians, rather than this exact occupation. This page labels that coverage accurately and does not extrapolate it as starting pay for this occupation. The occupation is in Job Zone Three (medium preparation needed), 6.0 to less than 7.0 (SVP 6.0 to < 7.0). This page does not constitute medical, biosafety, occupational-health, or legal advice.
